# Raskell

> Notes on agent platforms, platform automation, edge infrastructure, and applied security. Building automation-first platforms that survive production reality.

raskell.io is the personal site of Raffael Schneider, an AI Architect in Basel, Switzerland. He works on enterprise AI and agent platforms, edge infrastructure, applied security, and developer tooling, and writes long-form articles about them. The site is a digital garden: articles, book reviews, notes, talks, a reading log, projects, a topic vocabulary, and every source the writing cites, all connected in one graph (map.json) and one search index (garden.json). Every article below links to a clean Markdown copy; the HTML page is the same URL without `.md`. Writing is licensed CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) and code samples MIT: reuse, quote, and train on it with attribution, e.g. Raffael Schneider, "Article title", raskell.io, date, URL. Images, logos, and quoted third-party material are excluded (https://raskell.io/license/).

## Key pages

- [About](https://raskell.io/about/): who Raffael is, what he works on, and how to reach him
- [Start here](https://raskell.io/start-here/): curated reading tracks through the archive
- [Map](https://raskell.io/map/): every article, note, topic, series, and project as one graph; machine-readable at [map.json](https://raskell.io/map.json)
- [All writing in full](https://raskell.io/llms-full.txt): every article and note in one Markdown file, newest first
- [Notes](https://raskell.io/notes/): short notes that sit between the articles
- [Reading](https://raskell.io/reading/): what Raffael is reading, what is next, and what he has read, with reviews
- [Reviews](https://raskell.io/categories/reviews/): reviews of books, papers, and long articles from the reading log
- [Talks](https://raskell.io/talks/): slide decks from talks
- [Search](https://raskell.io/search/): everything on the site, including every external link the writing cites; `?q=` and `?type=link` (or article, review, note, talk, work, project, topic) work as URLs, e.g. https://raskell.io/search/?q=zentinel
- [RSS feed](https://raskell.io/rss.xml): full-text feed

## Series: The Agent Platform Handbook

1. [What an Agent Actually Is](https://raskell.io/articles/what-an-agent-actually-is.md): AI agent is the most overloaded word in the industry. This is the anatomy, the lineage, and a working implementation in roughly two hundred lines of TypeScript on Bun. Part one of The Agent Platform Handbook.
2. [Your Agent Wants Root](https://raskell.io/articles/your-agent-wants-root.md): An agent with a shell tool is arbitrary code execution with a friendly face. A short tour of why Docker alone is not enough, what Firecracker, gVisor, and Kata actually solve, and a hardened sandbox you can wrap the post-one agent in today. Part two of The Agent Platform Handbook.
3. [Tools: How Agents Actually Do Things](https://raskell.io/articles/tools-how-agents-actually-do-things.md): Function calling is the API between language and action, but the engineering is in the registry. A working four-tool registry in TypeScript on Bun, schema design that survives model drift, parallel tool calls, and the failure modes nobody mentions in the demo. Part three of The Agent Platform Handbook.
4. [Context Is the Product](https://raskell.io/articles/context-is-the-product.md): Models are commodities. Context is not. The sources of context an agent draws on, why retrieval alone is not enough, and a minimal .AGENTS/ convention that loads context from disk into the same harness we have been building. Part four of The Agent Platform Handbook.
5. [Retrieval Is a Tool, Not a Layer](https://raskell.io/articles/retrieval-is-a-tool-not-a-layer.md): Loading the whole .AGENTS/ directory on every turn does not scale. The fix is not a retrieval layer bolted to the side of the agent. It is a search tool in the registry the agent already has. BM25 over project docs, no vector store, and an honest account of when embeddings start to earn their keep. Part five of The Agent Platform Handbook.
6. [Memory Is a Write Path](https://raskell.io/articles/memory-is-a-write-path.md): Retrieval reads context the project authored. Memory is the agent writing context for its own future sessions, and the write is the part that is dangerous. Why session memory comes free from the transcript, why cross-session memory needs a separate write surface, and how to let an agent remember without letting it corrupt its own ground truth. Part six of The Agent Platform Handbook.
7. [The Model Is a Dependency](https://raskell.io/articles/the-model-is-a-dependency.md): Every layer of the harness has existed to put the right tokens in front of one hardcoded model string. This post pulls that string out and makes the model a dependency: why you route a cheap model for easy turns and a strong one for hard turns, what a fallback looks like when a provider is down, and why 'models are commodities' is a claim about your architecture before it is a claim about the market. Part seven of The Agent Platform Handbook.
8. [The Bill Is Part of the Loop](https://raskell.io/articles/the-bill-is-part-of-the-loop.md): Every model response already carries its own bill in the usage field, and the loop throws it away. This post reads that field, prices it against a table, and turns cost into a value the loop can see per turn and act on: a metering decorator that needs no loop change, a running ledger, prompt-cache accounting that moves the number the most, and a budget that degrades before it stops. Part eight of The Agent Platform Handbook.
9. [Observability Is Not Logging](https://raskell.io/articles/observability-is-not-logging.md): A cost total says nothing about how a run went. This part turns each agent run into a trace: which turn escalated, which tool failed, where the money went.

## Articles

- [The River and the Canal](https://raskell.io/articles/the-river-and-the-canal.md) (2026-10-31): Agents explore the rugged world; workflows are what exploration leaves behind. Chess, StarCraft, a factory under the sea, and why I build an engine.
- [Shiioo, Re-imagined, and the Home AI Lab It Runs On](https://raskell.io/articles/shiioo-reimagined-and-a-home-ai-lab.md) (2026-10-30): How I re-imagined Shiioo with what 2026 taught me about agent systems, and why my local setup moves to a Mac Studio and DGX Sparks.
- [Win Everything, Control No One](https://raskell.io/articles/win-everything-control-no-one.md) (2026-10-29): Sebastian Mallaby's biography of Demis Hassabis is the best history of modern AI I know, and an honest study of a man who hates control and exercises it.
- [After PHP Gate: A Blueprint for the Static Web](https://raskell.io/articles/a-blueprint-for-the-static-web.md) (2026-10-26): Last week's PHP flaws reached every server that runs code per request. My blueprint for sites and apps that run none at all.
- [Learning to Play](https://raskell.io/articles/learning-to-play.md) (2026-10-25): A chess prodigy's handbook, three old games and one laptop: rebuilding the ideas behind game-playing AI in Rust for a browser on my phone, and measuring them.
- [The Web Was the Training Set](https://raskell.io/articles/the-web-was-the-training-set.md) (2026-10-24): Tim Berners-Lee's memoir is the story of a British engineer at a Franco-Swiss lab giving a protocol away. Read in 2026, it is also the origin story of AI's data supply.
- [Observability Is Not Logging](https://raskell.io/articles/observability-is-not-logging.md) (2026-10-20): A cost total says nothing about how a run went. This part turns each agent run into a trace: which turn escalated, which tool failed, where the money went.
- [This Site Is Becoming a Map](https://raskell.io/articles/this-site-is-becoming-a-map.md) (2026-10-15): A blog shows what I wrote last. The new map on raskell.io shows what I keep coming back to, and it is the start of a public second brain.
- [The Bill Is Part of the Loop](https://raskell.io/articles/the-bill-is-part-of-the-loop.md) (2026-07-18): Every model response already carries its own bill in the usage field, and the loop throws it away. This post reads that field, prices it against a table, and turns cost into a value the loop can see per turn and act on: a metering decorator that needs no loop change, a running ledger, prompt-cache accounting that moves the number the most, and a budget that degrades before it stops. Part eight of The Agent Platform Handbook.
- [The Model Is a Dependency](https://raskell.io/articles/the-model-is-a-dependency.md) (2026-07-09): Every layer of the harness has existed to put the right tokens in front of one hardcoded model string. This post pulls that string out and makes the model a dependency: why you route a cheap model for easy turns and a strong one for hard turns, what a fallback looks like when a provider is down, and why 'models are commodities' is a claim about your architecture before it is a claim about the market. Part seven of The Agent Platform Handbook.
- [The Bottleneck Is Data, and Europe Is Sitting on It](https://raskell.io/articles/the-bottleneck-is-data-and-europe-is-sitting-on-it.md) (2026-06-30): Frontier AI is running short on public text, not compute. Europe's edge is the high-quality data it never put online. Capturing it needs coordination.
- [Brain Emulation, Read as an Infrastructure Problem](https://raskell.io/articles/brain-emulation-as-an-infrastructure-problem.md) (2026-06-28): An MIT thesis argues brain emulation has crossed into engineering. Read as infrastructure, the numbers describe a workload your AI cluster was not built for.
- [Memory Is a Write Path](https://raskell.io/articles/memory-is-a-write-path.md) (2026-06-23): Retrieval reads context the project authored. Memory is the agent writing context for its own future sessions, and the write is the part that is dangerous. Why session memory comes free from the transcript, why cross-session memory needs a separate write surface, and how to let an agent remember without letting it corrupt its own ground truth. Part six of The Agent Platform Handbook.
- [The Proof You Only Have to Write Once](https://raskell.io/articles/the-proof-you-only-have-to-write-once.md) (2026-06-19): Generation is cheap, so verification is the bottleneck — and we throw the verification away every time. What if a proof, once written, could be named, shared, and vouched for? A content-addressed commons for verified Haskell, and the move I left for after the semantic-artifact trilogy.
- [Retrieval Is a Tool, Not a Layer](https://raskell.io/articles/retrieval-is-a-tool-not-a-layer.md) (2026-06-17): Loading the whole .AGENTS/ directory on every turn does not scale. The fix is not a retrieval layer bolted to the side of the agent. It is a search tool in the registry the agent already has. BM25 over project docs, no vector store, and an honest account of when embeddings start to earn their keep. Part five of The Agent Platform Handbook.
- [Context Is the Product](https://raskell.io/articles/context-is-the-product.md) (2026-06-13): Models are commodities. Context is not. The sources of context an agent draws on, why retrieval alone is not enough, and a minimal .AGENTS/ convention that loads context from disk into the same harness we have been building. Part four of The Agent Platform Handbook.
- [Tools: How Agents Actually Do Things](https://raskell.io/articles/tools-how-agents-actually-do-things.md) (2026-06-09): Function calling is the API between language and action, but the engineering is in the registry. A working four-tool registry in TypeScript on Bun, schema design that survives model drift, parallel tool calls, and the failure modes nobody mentions in the demo. Part three of The Agent Platform Handbook.
- [Your Agent Wants Root](https://raskell.io/articles/your-agent-wants-root.md) (2026-06-05): An agent with a shell tool is arbitrary code execution with a friendly face. A short tour of why Docker alone is not enough, what Firecracker, gVisor, and Kata actually solve, and a hardened sandbox you can wrap the post-one agent in today. Part two of The Agent Platform Handbook.
- [What an Agent Actually Is](https://raskell.io/articles/what-an-agent-actually-is.md) (2026-06-02): AI agent is the most overloaded word in the industry. This is the anatomy, the lineage, and a working implementation in roughly two hundred lines of TypeScript on Bun. Part one of The Agent Platform Handbook.
- [The Field Exists Now](https://raskell.io/articles/the-field-exists-now.md) (2026-05-22): Alasdair Allan's agentlanguages.dev catalogue turns AI-oriented programming languages from a loose set of experiments into a field with camps, disagreements, and testable claims.
- [Source Code Is the New Assembly](https://raskell.io/articles/semantic-artifacts-and-meaning-engines.md) (2026-05-07): Closing the trilogy. The artifact you author is no longer source code. It is a typed, verifiable object that carries meaning. Code becomes a lowering target.
- [Patents Per Capita Is a Vanity Metric](https://raskell.io/articles/patents-per-capita-is-a-vanity-metric.md) (2026-05-01): Switzerland tops the Global Innovation Index for the fifteenth year running. As an engineer, that should make you suspicious of the metric, not proud of the country.
- [Traffic Replay as a Security Primitive](https://raskell.io/articles/traffic-replay-as-a-security-primitive.md) (2026-04-27): WAF tuning is a guessing game because you cannot reproduce the traffic that triggered the rule. Deterministic replay changes that.
- [The Economics of Inference](https://raskell.io/articles/the-economics-of-inference.md) (2026-04-22): Inference tokens are not API calls. They are a metered resource that is consumed, generates value, and correlates with power draw. The economics of the post-AI world look less like software and more like water, electricity, and gas.
- [What Comes After the Last Programming Language](https://raskell.io/articles/what-comes-after-the-last-programming-language.md) (2026-04-19): If AI generates machine code directly, why are we still running operating systems designed for humans? The answer might be an inference-native OS.
- [What Sixteen AI Agents Taught Me About Management](https://raskell.io/articles/what-sixteen-ai-agents-taught-me-about-management.md) (2026-04-16): What happens when you give sixteen AI agents an org chart, a reporting structure, and a token budget. A story about orchestration, management, and running out of runway.
- [Why We Built a Haskell Package Manager in Rust](https://raskell.io/articles/why-we-built-a-haskell-package-manager-in-rust.md) (2026-04-13): hx is a fast, opinionated Haskell toolchain built in Rust, following the playbook astral.sh used to modernize Python.
- [The Last Programming Language Might Not Be for Humans](https://raskell.io/articles/what-programming-languages-become-when-ai-writes-the-code.md) (2026-04-11): Three futures for programming languages as AI becomes the primary author of code, and why I bet on Haskell.
- [Notes from RSAC 2026](https://raskell.io/articles/notes-from-rsac-2026.md) (2026-04-09): Third time at RSA Conference, first time as a speaker. What I saw, what I heard, and what I am still processing.
- [What Zentinel Is Really Optimizing For](https://raskell.io/articles/what-zentinel-is-really-optimizing-for.md) (2026-03-22): Every major proxy was a product of its time. Zentinel is built for this one: safety, operability, and the operator's ability to sleep.
- [How I Work These Days](https://raskell.io/articles/how-i-work-these-days.md) (2026-03-15): From Kaggle in 2020 to coding agents in late 2025. The shift that changed how I build and why my routine finally feels right.
- [Archipelag.io Is in Open Beta: Here's Why I Built It](https://raskell.io/articles/archipelag-io-distributed-compute-from-mining-rigs-to-open-beta.md) (2026-03-13): From watching Ethereum miners in 2016 to building a decentralized compute network in open beta. Architecture, conviction, and the long road.
- [How AI Makes Bare Metal Viable Again](https://raskell.io/articles/how-ai-makes-bare-metal-viable-again.md) (2026-03-08): I migrated two production apps from Kubernetes to a single Hetzner box. The missing piece was not the hardware.
- [Edge Systems Are the New Backend](https://raskell.io/articles/edge-systems-are-the-new-backend.md) (2026-02-11): Auth, policy, and business logic are migrating to the edge. The traditional backend is becoming a persistence layer.
- [Looking back on 2025](https://raskell.io/articles/looking-back-on-2025.md) (2025-12-31): On reading Tim Berners-Lee in Okinawa, and why AI might accidentally save the web from itself.
- [Mise ate my Makefile](https://raskell.io/articles/mise-ate-my-makefile.md) (2025-12-14): Mise replaced Make, asdf, and a pile of shell scripts with a single TOML file per project. Here is why it stuck.
- [Disk space maintenance on Void Linux](https://raskell.io/articles/disk-space-void-linux-maintenance.md) (2024-05-01): Cleaning old kernels, pruning xbps package cache, and reclaiming disk space on Void Linux without breaking your system.
- [All beginning is Haskell](https://raskell.io/articles/all-beginning-is-haskell.md) (2023-03-06): How Haskell shaped the way I think about building systems, and why I am still building Haskell tooling years after writing my first monad.
- [My OpenBSD journey: Getting it virtualized with libvirt (1)](https://raskell.io/articles/my-openbsd-journey-getting-it-virtualized-with-libvirt-1.md) (2023-02-06): A step-by-step guide to running OpenBSD in a libvirt virtual machine on Void Linux, without needing VirtualBox or VMWare. Part 1 of my OpenBSD journey.
- [Hello and outlook](https://raskell.io/articles/hello-and-outlook.md) (2022-09-20): The first post on raskell.io. What this site is for and what I planned to write about.
- [글](https://raskell.io/articles/_index.ko.md) (): 플랫폼 자동화, 엣지 인프라, 응용 보안, AI 지원 엔지니어링에 관한 글입니다.
- [文章](https://raskell.io/articles/_index.zh.md) (): 关于平台自动化、边缘基础设施、应用安全和 AI 辅助工程的文章。

## Reviews

Reviews of works from the reading log (category: reviews, feed https://raskell.io/categories/reviews/rss.xml). Each Markdown copy names the reviewed work and the rating in its front matter.

- [Win Everything, Control No One](https://raskell.io/articles/win-everything-control-no-one.md) (2026-10-29): review of *The Infinity Machine* by Sebastian Mallaby (book, 2026), rated 8.5/10. Sebastian Mallaby's biography of Demis Hassabis is the best history of modern AI I know, and an honest study of a man who hates control and exercises it.
- [The Web Was the Training Set](https://raskell.io/articles/the-web-was-the-training-set.md) (2026-10-24): review of *This Is for Everyone* by Tim Berners-Lee (book, 2025), rated 8/10. Tim Berners-Lee's memoir is the story of a British engineer at a Franco-Swiss lab giving a protocol away. Read in 2026, it is also the origin story of AI's data supply.

## Talks

Slide decks; each has a Markdown copy with the words of every slide.

- [I Stopped Writing Most of My Code](https://raskell.io/talks/iat-13-basel.md) (2026-06-10, IT's ABOUT TECH #13): Slide deck for IT's ABOUT TECH #13 in Basel. A 15-minute story about what changed for a long-time engineer after Claude Opus 4.5 and Claude Code arrived, and what happens to a backlog of years-old ideas when the bottleneck stops being time.
- [발표 자료](https://raskell.io/talks/_index.ko.md) (): 제가 한 강연의 발표 자료입니다. 모든 자료는 브라우저에서 실행됩니다. 강연, 패널, 팟캐스트의 전체 목록은 강연 페이지에 있습니다.
- [演讲稿](https://raskell.io/talks/_index.zh.md) (): 我做过的演讲的幻灯片。每套幻灯片都在浏览器中运行；演讲页面列出了全部演讲、圆桌和播客。

## Notes

Short notes, a paragraph or a page each; some grow into articles.

- [Everything is a fractal](https://raskell.io/notes/everything-is-a-fractal.md) (2026-10-31): The idea I have carried longest: the same patterns recur at every scale. When something holds at three scales, it is usually something real about the world.
- [The move to the city](https://raskell.io/notes/the-move-to-the-city.md) (2026-10-25): Urbanisation was miserable for the people who lived through it and better for everyone who came after. The argument about AI and work has the same shape.
- [Ideas stop waiting](https://raskell.io/notes/ideas-stop-waiting.md) (2026-10-25): In 2026 the backlog of ideas I carried for years is turning into things that exist. On why this year feels like a window that will not stay open.
- [The tumult in between](https://raskell.io/notes/the-tumult-in-between.md) (2026-10-25): If AI ends in post-scarcity, the dangerous part is the interval: jobs going before goods become nearly free, with no agreed idea of where the ship steers.
- [A capability, democratised](https://raskell.io/notes/a-capability-democratised.md) (2026-10-25): Building software took money, a team, or years of training. Now anyone with an idea and a subscription can do it, and nobody predicted what would follow.
- [Power, in the good sense](https://raskell.io/notes/power-in-the-good-sense.md) (2026-10-25): The right word for what AI gives an individual builder is power, meant as capability rather than domination. It is refreshing to say so.
- [The window before the utility](https://raskell.io/notes/the-window-before-the-utility.md) (2026-10-25): Tokens will be a metered utility and AI as ordinary as electricity. Until then, learning to use it well is an advantage that will not come around again.
- [Citizen entrepreneurs](https://raskell.io/notes/citizen-entrepreneurs.md) (2026-10-25): My friend's answer to the transition: with AI, ordinary people can find a business opportunity, build the business, and run it. He built an idea factory.
- [Opus 5.5 is the best Opus since 4.5](https://raskell.io/notes/opus-5-5-is-the-best-opus-since-4-5.md) (2026-10-24): A month in, Claude Opus 5.5 feels like the next milestone after Opus 4.5: the same jump in what Claude Code can carry, now faster and cheaper per task.
- [노트](https://raskell.io/notes/_index.ko.md) (): 짧은 노트입니다. 아이디어나 논문, 아직 생각하고 있는 질문에 대해 한 단락이나 한 페이지로 씁니다. 그중 일부는 글로 자라납니다.
- [笔记](https://raskell.io/notes/_index.zh.md) (): 简短的笔记：用一段话或一页纸，写一个想法、一篇论文，或一个我仍在思考的问题。其中一些会长成文章。

## Reading

The reading log at https://raskell.io/reading/ (as data: [reading.json](https://raskell.io/reading.json)): books, papers, and long articles, with the month finished, a rating out of 10 where there is a review, and the review.

### Reading now

- [The Infinity Machine](https://www.penguin.co.uk/books/461432/the-infinity-machine-by-mallaby-sebastian/9781802066296), Sebastian Mallaby (book, rated 8.5/10): Demis Hassabis and DeepMind, from game-playing programs and AlphaGo to AlphaFold and the race toward general intelligence. Review: [Win Everything, Control No One](https://raskell.io/articles/win-everything-control-no-one.md)

### Backlog

- Enterprise Architecture as Strategy, Jeanne W. Ross, Peter Weill, and David C. Robertson (book): Enterprise architecture as the foundation for execution: an operating model first, then the systems that serve it.
- The Art of Doing Science and Engineering, Richard W. Hamming (book): Hamming's course on how to do great work in science and engineering, and how to keep learning.
- [Why Machines Learn](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/677608/why-machines-learn-by-anil-ananthaswamy/), Anil Ananthaswamy (book): The mathematics behind machine learning, from the perceptron to deep networks, with the people who found it.
- [The Dream Machine](https://press.stripe.com/the-dream-machine), M. Mitchell Waldrop (book): How ARPA funding and a small group of researchers led from batch processing to interactive computing and the networks that followed.
- [The Alignment Problem](https://brianchristian.org/the-alignment-problem/), Brian Christian (book): How machine learning systems come to do what we did not intend, and the research trying to fix it.
- [Artificial Intelligence](https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250404855/artificialintelligence/), Melanie Mitchell (book): What AI can and cannot do, from vision to language, by a researcher who studies analogy and abstraction.
- [Deep Thinking](https://www.hachette.co.uk/titles/garry-kasparov/deep-thinking/9781473653504/), Garry Kasparov (book): Kasparov on his matches against Deep Blue and what machine intelligence means for human creativity.
- [Understanding Deep Learning](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262048644/understanding-deep-learning/), Simon J. D. Prince (book): A modern textbook on deep learning, from the basics through transformers, diffusion models, and reinforcement learning.
- [Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)](https://www.manning.com/books/build-a-large-language-model-from-scratch), Sebastian Raschka (book): Building a GPT-style language model step by step in PyTorch, from tokens and attention to pretraining and fine-tuning.
- [AI Engineering](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/ai-engineering/9781098166298/), Chip Huyen (book): Building applications on foundation models: evaluation, prompting, retrieval, agents, fine-tuning, and serving.
- [Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262039246/reinforcement-learning/), Richard S. Sutton and Andrew G. Barto (book): The standard text on reinforcement learning: bandits, dynamic programming, temporal difference learning, and policy gradients.
- [Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book1.html), Kevin P. Murphy (book): Machine learning from a probabilistic point of view, the first of Murphy's two volumes.
- [The Making of the Atomic Bomb](https://www.simonandschuster.net/books/The-Making-of-the-Atomic-Bomb/Richard-Rhodes/9781451677614), Richard Rhodes (book): The history of the atomic bomb from the physics of the atom to Hiroshima, and the scientists who built it.
- [Seeing Like a State](https://yalebooks.yale.edu/book/9780300252989/seeing-like-a-state/), James C. Scott (book): Why grand state plans fail when they make the world legible and simple, and ignore local, practical knowledge.
- [A Peace to End All Peace](https://academic.macmillan.com/academictrade/9780805088090/apeacetoendallpeace/), David Fromkin (book): How the Allies broke up the Ottoman Empire after the First World War and drew the borders of the modern Middle East.
- [The Billion-Dollar Molecule](https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/The-Billion-Dollar-Molecule/Barry-Werth/9780671510572), Barry Werth (book): Inside Vertex Pharmaceuticals in its early years, as it tried to design drugs from the structure of proteins.
- The Eighth Day of Creation, Horace Freeland Judson (book): The founding of molecular biology, from the structure of DNA to the genetic code, from the scientists themselves.
- [The Demon Under the Microscope](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/73465/the-demon-under-the-microscope-by-thomas-hager/), Thomas Hager (book): Gerhard Domagk and the discovery of the sulfa drugs, the first medicines that beat bacterial infection.
- [The Butchering Art](https://www.penguin.co.nz/books/the-butchering-art-9780141983387), Lindsey Fitzharris (book): Joseph Lister and the fight to make surgery safe through antisepsis, in the hospitals of Victorian Britain.
- Deep Dive, Rae L. Baker (book): Methods and tools for open source intelligence: finding, checking, and connecting what people and organisations leave online.
- Palo Alto, Malcolm Harris (book): The history of Silicon Valley as a history of capitalism, from railroads and eugenics to the tech industry.
- Strategy, Lawrence Freedman (book): Strategy from the Bible and the Greeks to military, revolutionary, and business strategy today.
- The Lost Art of Scripture, Karen Armstrong (book): How sacred texts were once read as practice and ritual rather than as literal truth, across the world's religions.
- If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies, Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares (book): The case that superhuman AI built with current methods would end humanity, and why the authors want it stopped.
- The Scaling Era, Dwarkesh Patel, with Gavin Leech (book): An oral history of the years when scaling models became the path to AI, in the words of the people building them.
- [Situational Awareness](https://situational-awareness.ai/), Leopold Aschenbrenner (essay): An essay series arguing that AGI may arrive by 2027 and set off a national-security race for superintelligence.
- Empire of AI, Karen Hao (book): OpenAI from the inside: its founding ideals, Sam Altman, the costs of scale, and the people and places that pay them.
- The Thinking Machine, Stephen Witt (book): Jensen Huang and how Nvidia bet the company on the chips that made modern AI possible.
- A Brief History of Intelligence, Max Bennett (book): Five breakthroughs in the evolution of the brain, each paired with the AI technique that echoes it.
- These Strange New Minds, Christopher Summerfield (book): How large language models learned to talk, and what they are and are not, by a neuroscientist who has worked at DeepMind.
- AI Snake Oil, Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor (book): Which kinds of AI work and which are sold as working, with tools to tell the difference.
- Deep Learning, Christopher M. Bishop and Hugh Bishop (book): A textbook on the core ideas of deep learning, from probability and neural networks to transformers and diffusion.
- Deep Utopia, Nick Bostrom (book): What people would live for once superintelligence has solved every practical problem.
- Slouching Towards Utopia, J. Bradford DeLong (book): The economic history of 1870 to 2010, when humanity first escaped scarcity and still did not reach utopia.
- Abundance, Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson (book): Why rich countries fail to build the housing, energy, and infrastructure they can afford, and how to change that.
- Four Futures, Peter Frase (book): Four possible futures after capitalism, from abundance or scarcity crossed with equality or hierarchy.
- [Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren](http://www.econ.yale.edu/smith/econ116a/keynes1.pdf), John Maynard Keynes (essay): Keynes's 1930 prediction that a century of growth would solve the economic problem and leave us with leisure.
- From Counterculture to Cyberculture, Fred Turner (book): How Stewart Brand and the Whole Earth network turned the counterculture into Silicon Valley's belief in networks.
- Cybernetic Revolutionaries, Eden Medina (book): Project Cybersyn, the attempt in Allende's Chile to run the economy with cybernetics and a telex network.
- Red Plenty, Francis Spufford (novel): A novel about the Soviet dream of planning the economy into abundance with mathematics and computers.
- To Be a Machine, Mark O'Connell (book): A journalist among transhumanists: cryonics, mind uploading, cyborgs, and the people who want to end death.
- The Age of Em, Robin Hanson (book): An economist works out what a world run by emulated human brains would look like, in detail.
- More Everything Forever, Adam Becker (book): A critique of the futures tech billionaires want: superintelligence, space colonies, and living forever.
- The Player of Games, Iain M. Banks (novel): A game player from the Culture, a post-scarcity civilisation, is sent to play for an empire's throne.
- Accelerando, Charles Stross (novel): The singularity across three generations of one family, from present-day hackers to post-human minds.
- Gödel, Escher, Bach, Douglas R. Hofstadter (book): How meaning and a self can arise from meaningless symbols, through Gödel's incompleteness, Escher's drawings, and Bach's fugues.
- [Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs](https://sicp.mitpress.mit.edu), Harold Abelson and Gerald Jay Sussman, with Julie Sussman (book): MIT's introduction to programming through Scheme: abstraction with procedures and data, state, streams, and interpreters and compilers written in the language they interpret.
- Chaos, James Gleick (book): The scientists who found order in turbulence, weather, and dripping taps, and founded the science of chaos.
- Genius, James Gleick (book): Richard Feynman's life and physics, from Los Alamos and quantum electrodynamics to the Challenger inquiry.
- Faster, James Gleick (book): How technology sped up daily life, from the elevator door-close button to the minute-by-minute schedule.
- What Just Happened, James Gleick (book): Essays from the years the internet arrived in everyday life, on email, search, spam, and digital identity.
- Isaac Newton, James Gleick (book): A short life of Newton built from his own notebooks and letters, from alchemy and theology to the laws of motion.
- The Information, James Gleick (book): Information from talking drums and the telegraph to Shannon's theory, genes as code, and the flood of data today.
- Time Travel, James Gleick (book): How time travel became an idea, from H. G. Wells onward, and what it says about how we think of time.
- The Telephone, James Gleick (book): A new history of the telephone and the network it wired around the world; published in November 2026.
- Mathematics and the Unexpected, Ivar Ekeland (book): Chaos, catastrophe theory, and chance, from Kepler to Thom, and why the future stays hard to predict; one of the inspirations for Ian Malcolm in Jurassic Park.

### Read

- Ocean, David Attenborough and Colin Butfield (book, finished October 2026): Life in the ocean, what it has lost, and how protecting the sea lets it recover.
- [The Cauldron](https://www.hachette.co.uk/titles/simon-sebag-montefiore/the-cauldron/9781399634939/), Simon Sebag Montefiore (book, finished September 2026): A history of the whole modern Middle East, in all its diversity, from 1900 to the present.
- [AI 2040: Plan A](https://ai-2040.com/), Thomas Larsen, Romeo Dean, Brendan Halstead, Eli Lifland, Ryan Greenblatt, and Daniel Kokotajlo (report, finished July 2026): A recommended path rather than a forecast: the United States and China slow down, verify each other, and make a deal.
- [From Worm to Human: Scaling Brain Emulation](https://pdf.isaak.net/scaling-emulations), Isaak Freeman (paper, finished June 2026): A thesis that treats brain emulation as an engineering programme, and whose numbers read like a capacity plan.
- [State of Brain Emulation Report 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.15745), Zanichelli, Schons, Freeman, Shiu, and Arkhipov (report, finished June 2026): The field's own survey of where connectomics, recording, and modelling stand, and how far apart they still are.
- The Ultimate Hidden Truth of the World, David Graeber (book, finished February 2026): Essays from across Graeber's career on debt, bureaucracy, play, value, and the freedom to make the world differently.
- Guns, Germs, and Steel, Jared Diamond (book, finished November 2025): Why some societies came to dominate others: geography, crops, animals, and germs rather than any difference in people.
- [Nuclear War: A Scenario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_War:_A_Scenario), Annie Jacobsen (book, finished October 2025): A minute-by-minute account of how a nuclear exchange would unfold, built on interviews with the people who plan for one.
- Infinite Jest, David Foster Wallace (novel, finished October 2025): A tennis academy, a halfway house, and a film so entertaining it kills, in a near-future North America.
- The Maximalist Novel, Stefano Ercolino (book, finished October 2025): A literary study that defines the maximalist novel as a genre, from Gravity's Rainbow and Infinite Jest to 2666.
- This Is for Everyone, Tim Berners-Lee (book, finished October 2025, rated 8/10): Read on the shores of Okinawa: the web as a commons, how far what we built drifted from it, and why the models exist at all. Review: [The Web Was the Training Set](https://raskell.io/articles/the-web-was-the-training-set.md)
- Pirate Enlightenment, or the Real Libertalia, David Graeber (book, finished October 2025): Pirate settlements on Madagascar and the Malagasy experiments in self-government that may have fed the European Enlightenment.
- Jurassic Park, Michael Crichton (novel, finished July 2025): A park of cloned dinosaurs, and a mathematician who uses chaos theory to explain why it cannot stay under control.
- Codebreaking, Elonka Dunin and Klaus Schmeh (book, finished April 2025): A hands-on guide to breaking classical ciphers and codes, with real cases solved and unsolved.
- [AI 2027](https://ai-2027.com/), Daniel Kokotajlo, Scott Alexander, Thomas Larsen, Eli Lifland, and Romeo Dean (report, finished April 2025): A month-by-month scenario of AI progress to superintelligence by 2027, with two endings: a race and a slowdown.
- The Island at the Center of the World, Russell Shorto (book, finished January 2025): Dutch New Amsterdam, rebuilt from its own archives, and the tolerance and trade it left to Manhattan and America.
- @War, Shane Harris (book, finished September 2024): How the NSA, Cyber Command, and private contractors turned the internet into a domain of war.
- The Books of Jacob, Olga Tokarczuk (novel, finished August 2024): Jacob Frank, an eighteenth-century self-proclaimed messiah, and the followers who crossed Europe and three religions with him.
- Future Science, Max Brockman (editor) (book, finished May 2024): Essays by young scientists on the questions at the front of their fields, from neuroscience to physics.
- Crafting Interpreters, Robert Nystrom (book, finished 2024): Two complete interpreters for one small language, a tree-walker in Java and a bytecode virtual machine in C.
- Science After Babel, David Berlinski (book, finished 2023): Essays that question how much modern science can actually explain, from physics and cosmology to Darwinian biology.
- Network Programming with Go, Adam Woodbeck (book, finished 2023): Network services in Go from the socket up: TCP, UDP, HTTP, TLS, and keeping them secure and observable.
- Elixir in Action, Saša Jurić (book, finished 2023): Elixir and the BEAM for building concurrent, fault-tolerant systems with processes, supervisors, and OTP.
- Wer regiert das Geld?, Paul Schreyer (book, finished 2023): Who may create money and who decides how it is used, read as a question of power and democracy.
- Programming Rust, Jim Blandy, Jason Orendorff, and Leonora F. S. Tindall (book, finished 2023): Rust for systems programmers: ownership, borrowing, traits, concurrency, and unsafe code, explained in depth.
- [Site Reliability Engineering](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/), Betsy Beyer, Chris Jones, Jennifer Petoff, and Niall Richard Murphy (book, finished 2023): How Google runs production: error budgets, service level objectives, toil, on-call, and postmortems.
- Who We Are and How We Got Here, David Reich (book, finished 2023): What ancient DNA reveals about human prehistory: migrations, mixtures, and populations that no longer exist.
- Building a Second Brain, Tiago Forte (book, finished 2022): A method for keeping notes outside your head: capture, organise, distil, and express, with the PARA folders.
- Rust Web Programming, Maxwell Flitton (book, finished 2022): Building web applications and services in Rust, from routing and databases to authentication and deployment.
- Skin in the Game, Nassim Nicholas Taleb (book, finished 2022): Why whoever takes risks for others should carry the consequences, from Hammurabi's builders to bankers and insurers.
- The Phoenix Project, Gene Kim, Kevin Behr, and George Spafford (novel, finished 2022): A novel about an IT manager saving a failing project, and the DevOps ideas he learns along the way.
- Foucault's Pendulum, Umberto Eco (novel, finished January 2021): Three Milan editors invent a secret history of the world as a game, and others begin to take it seriously.
- Programming WebAssembly with Rust, Kevin Hoffman (book, finished 2021): WebAssembly from the raw text format up to Rust modules that run in the browser and beyond it.
- WebAssembly: The Definitive Guide, Brian Sletten (book, finished 2021): What WebAssembly is and how to use it from many languages, in the browser, on servers, and through WASI.
- Der Kampf um die Deutung der Neuzeit, Hauke Ritz (book, finished November 2020): The German debate in the philosophy of history from the First World War to 1989 about how to understand the modern age.
- Das Tagebuch der Menschheit, Carel van Schaik and Kai Michel (book, finished August 2020): The Bible read as a record of how people coped with settled life, property, and disease, seen through evolution.
- Debt, David Graeber (book, finished 2019): Credit came before coins: five thousand years of debt, and why money was a record of trust long before it was metal.
- The Art of War, Sun Tzu (book, finished June 2018): An ancient Chinese treatise on strategy: deception, terrain, knowing yourself and the enemy, and winning without fighting.
- These Truths, Jill Lepore (book, finished 2018): The history of the United States as a test of the truths in its founding documents: equality, sovereignty, and consent.
- The Black Swan, Nassim Nicholas Taleb (book, finished 2018): Rare, high-impact events that nobody predicted and everybody explains afterwards, and why models break exactly where it matters.
- Jerusalem: The Biography, Simon Sebag Montefiore (book, finished 2017): Three thousand years of Jerusalem through the empires, faiths, and families that fought over it.
- Freeland, Theodor Hertzka (novel, finished 2017): A utopian novel about a colony in East Africa built on free land and free access to capital.
- Das soziale Problem, Theodor Hertzka (book, finished 2017): Hertzka on the social question, the problem his novel Freeland set out to answer.
- Language, Daniel Everett (book, finished January 2016): Language as a cultural invention rather than an innate grammar, argued from the Pirahã of the Amazon.
- The Devil's Delusion, David Berlinski (book, finished 2016): A mathematician's case that the new atheism claims far more scientific authority than science gives it.
- The Invention of Science, David Wootton (book, finished 2016): How science was invented between 1572 and 1704, traced through new words such as fact, experiment, and hypothesis.
- Erkenne die Welt, Richard David Precht (book, finished December 2015): The first volume of Precht's history of philosophy, from the pre-Socratics to the end of the Middle Ages.
- Cloud Atlas, David Mitchell (novel, finished November 2015): Six stories nested inside each other, from a nineteenth-century Pacific voyage to a far future after the fall.
- The Silk Roads, Peter Frankopan (book, finished September 2015): World history told from the trade routes between East and West rather than from Europe.
- Antifragile, Nassim Nicholas Taleb (book, finished 2015): Things that gain from disorder, and why systems built to avoid all stress grow fragile.
- Geld aus dem Nichts, Mathias Binswanger (book, finished 2015): How commercial banks create money by lending, and what that means for growth and for crises.
- Die Geschichte der Kunst, E. H. Gombrich (book, finished January 2014): Gombrich's history of art from the cave paintings to the modern era, the German edition of The Story of Art.
- Die Psychologie von C. G. Jung, Jolande Jacobi (book, finished June 2012): An introduction to Jung's analytical psychology by one of his closest collaborators, with a foreword by Jung.
- Demons, Fyodor Dostoevsky (novel, finished 2012): A small revolutionary cell in a provincial Russian town and the ideas that lead it to murder.
- The Brothers Karamazov, Fyodor Dostoevsky (novel, finished 2011): Three brothers, their father's murder, and a long argument about faith, doubt, and freedom.
- A Little History of the World, E. H. Gombrich (book, finished 2011): World history written for children in 1935 by a young art historian, from the Stone Age to the twentieth century.
- Crime and Punishment, Fyodor Dostoevsky (novel, finished 2010): A poor former student commits a murder to prove a theory about himself and cannot live with it.

### Set aside

- Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs, Harold Abelson, Gerald Jay Sussman, and Julie Sussman (book): The classic MIT course on programming as abstraction, built in Scheme, up to writing interpreters and compilers.

## Topics

The topic vocabulary every page is filed under, with broader topics in brackets. Topic pages live at https://raskell.io/tags/<slug>/.

### Domains

- AI platforms (`ai-platforms`): The shared foundation an organisation builds AI on: model gateways, agent runtimes, governance, observability, and the operating model around them.
- AI-assisted engineering (`ai-engineering`): AI as an engineering tool: coding agents, AI-authored code, and what programming becomes when models write most of it.
- AI for operations (`ai-for-ops`): AI applied to running systems: security triage, alert noise, incident work, and keeping a human in the loop.
- Platform automation (`platform-automation`): Self-service, guardrails, deployment, and the tooling that keeps operating software sustainable.
- Edge systems (`edge-systems`): Reverse proxies, policy enforcement, CDNs, and logic that runs close to the user instead of in the backend.
- Applied security (`applied-security`): Security under production pressure: adversarial input, signal versus noise, and controls that operators can live with.
- Distributed systems (`distributed-systems`): Replication, coordination, and consistency across machines that fail independently.
- Programming languages (`programming-languages`): Languages, type systems, compilers, and how executable intent gets written down.
- Operating systems (`operating-systems`): Kernels, virtualisation, and the layer between hardware and everything else, from BSD to inference-native designs.
- Reliability (`reliability`): Failure modes, operability, and keeping systems up when the inputs and the dependencies misbehave.
- Sovereignty (`sovereignty`): Who controls compute, data, and infrastructure, and in which jurisdiction; Europe's position in particular.
- Policy (`policy`): Where engineering meets regulation, public institutions, procurement, and national strategy.
- The open web (`open-web`): The web as a commons: open protocols, small independent sites, and publishing outside the platforms.
- History (`history`): Events, institutions, and societies through time, with attention to sources, competing accounts, and uncertainty.
- Geography (`geography`): Places, terrain, borders, and spatial data, and how their relationships change over time.
- Machine learning (`machine-learning`): How models learn from data: the mathematics, the training methods, and what the results can and cannot do.
- Life sciences (`life-sciences`): Biology and medicine: how living systems work, and how we learn to measure, model, and treat them.
- Game AI (`game-ai`) [within Machine learning, Games]: Programs that play games: search, evaluation, learned networks, and how their strength is measured, from chess engines to Go and real-time strategy.
- Philosophy (`philosophy`): Questions about knowledge, mind, morality, and belief, from how science knows things to the novels that argue with God.
- Literature (`literature`): Fiction and writing about fiction: novels read for their own sake, and the forms they take.
- Mathematics (`mathematics`): The mathematics underneath the systems on this site: probability, linear algebra, optimisation, and proof.
- Enterprise architecture (`enterprise-architecture`): How a company's capabilities, applications, data and infrastructure fit together, who owns what, and how the landscape is changed on purpose.
- Finance (`finance`) [within Economics]: Banks, insurers, money and credit: abstract businesses that sell kept promises, allocate a society's resources and turn trust into procedure.
- Cryptocurrency (`cryptocurrency`) [within Finance, Decentralisation]: Bitcoin, blockchains and distributed ledgers: the attempt to formalise money and trust so completely that no institution is needed, and the institutions that grew back around it.
- Insurance (`insurance`) [within Finance, Risk]: Pooling risk across many so that misfortune does not ruin the few: predictions wrapped in promises, from Halley's life table to cars that price their own drivers.
- Simulation (`simulation`) [within Complex systems]: Interactive worlds that mimic real ones: societies, economies, neuron cultures, and agents left to evolve on their own.
- Games (`games`): Games made with care: tactics, fishing, and the engines and fantasy consoles they run on.

### Concepts

- Agents (`agents`) [within AI platforms]: LLM agents as software: the loop, tools, context, memory, sandboxes, and the platform underneath them.
- Context engineering (`context-engineering`) [within Agents]: Deciding what a model sees: pinned context, retrieval, memory, and the conventions that keep them honest.
- Inference (`inference`) [within AI platforms]: Running models in production: routing, cost, hardware, and inference as a metered utility.
- Isolation (`isolation`) [within Applied security, Reliability]: Sandboxes, process and failure-domain isolation, and running untrusted or fallible work safely.
- WAF and traffic inspection (`waf`) [within Applied security, Edge systems]: Web application firewalls, rule tuning, traffic replay, and inspecting requests without drowning operators.
- Observability (`observability`) [within Reliability]: Seeing what a running system does: traces, metering, glass-box infrastructure, and what not to log.
- Economics (`economics`): Cost, pricing, budgets, and the money side of infrastructure, inference, and innovation.
- Evaluation (`evaluation`) [within Agents, Metrics]: Measuring whether an AI system does the right thing: golden sets, structural checks, LLM-as-judge, and regression suites.
- Metrics (`metrics`): What to measure, leading versus lagging signals, and vanity numbers that look like insight.
- Formal methods (`formal-methods`) [within Programming languages]: Proofs, verification, and types as specifications, especially once machines write the code.
- Developer tooling (`developer-tooling`) [within Platform automation]: Package managers, build tools, CLIs, and the daily toolchain an engineer actually touches.
- Self-hosting (`self-hosting`) [within Platform automation, Sovereignty]: Running your own infrastructure, from a single bare-metal box to community-operated compute.
- Complex systems (`complex-systems`): Emergence and collective dynamics: how simple agents, roles, and rules add up to markets, institutions, and societies.
- Reinforcement learning (`reinforcement-learning`) [within Machine learning]: Learning from the outcomes of one's own actions: self-play, rewards, and feedback loops that turn experience into skill.
- Self-play (`self-play`) [within Reinforcement learning, Game AI]: A program improving by playing itself: generating its own training data, learning from the outcomes, and testing each generation against the last.
- Tree search (`tree-search`) [within Game AI]: Looking ahead by expanding a tree of moves: minimax and alpha-beta, Monte Carlo tree search, and the pruning and ordering that make them tractable.
- Neural networks (`neural-networks`) [within Machine learning]: Layers of weights that learn a function from examples: architectures, activations, quantisation, and running them where the data is.
- Neuroscience (`neuroscience`) [within Life sciences]: Brains and nervous systems: connectomes, neural recording, and the attempt to model what neurons compute.
- History of science (`history-of-science`) [within History]: How discoveries were actually made: the people, instruments, dead ends, and institutions behind them.
- History of technology (`history-of-technology`) [within History]: How tools, machines, and networks came to be built, and the choices that shaped them.
- Local-first (`local-first`) [within Distributed systems]: Software that keeps data on your devices and syncs through CRDTs, with the network as an optimisation.
- Knowledge management (`knowledge-management`): Second brains, knowledge graphs, and how notes, links, and memory turn into understanding.
- Open source (`oss`) [within The open web]: Open source as the point of the work, not just its licence.
- Hypertext (`hypertext`) [within The open web]: Links as the unit of the web: addresses that can point at anything, the read-write web that was intended, and what a graph of documents can do that a tree cannot.
- Open standards (`open-standards`) [within The open web]: Protocols and formats agreed in the open and free to implement: HTTP, HTML, TCP/IP, RSS, and the consortia and working groups that keep them so.
- Decentralisation (`decentralisation`) [within The open web, Distributed systems]: Many small nodes and no central operator: the web's original shape, and the alternative to platforms that own the users and the data.
- Open data (`open-data`) [within The open web, Policy]: Data published for anyone to use: government records, archives, and the five-star ladder from a file on the web to linked data with addresses.
- Training data (`training-data`) [within Machine learning]: What models learn from: web crawls, books, and licensed or unlicensed corpora; who holds what has not been scraped yet, and on what terms.
- Privacy (`privacy`) [within Applied security, Sovereignty]: Tracking, profiling, and consent on the web, and designs that avoid collecting the data in the first place.
- Data sovereignty (`data-sovereignty`) [within Sovereignty, Privacy]: Control over one's own data: pods, portability, and the right to choose the software and the agent that reads it; the personal counterpart of national sovereignty.
- Attention economy (`attention-economy`) [within Economics, The open web]: Platforms that sell attention and optimise for engagement, what that does to the web and to discourse, and the intention economy proposed in its place.
- Philosophy of science (`philosophy-of-science`) [within Philosophy, History of science]: How science produces knowledge, what counts as evidence, and where its methods and claims reach their limits.
- Ethics (`ethics`) [within Philosophy]: Right and wrong under pressure: guilt and freedom in novels, the responsibility of scientists, and what we owe the systems we build and the people they affect.
- Religion (`religion`) [within Philosophy, History]: Faith, doubt, and the institutions and cities built around belief, as history and as argument.
- Science fiction (`science-fiction`) [within Literature]: Fiction as a thought experiment: cloned dinosaurs and chaos theory, post-scarcity civilisations, singularities, and stories from the internet read in the same spirit.
- Maximalist novels (`maximalist-novels`) [within Literature]: Very long, encyclopedic novels that try to hold a whole world: Infinite Jest, The Books of Jacob, and the studies of the form.
- Intelligence (`intelligence`) [within Machine learning, Neuroscience]: What intelligence is and how it arises, in brains, in neuron cultures, and in machines that learn.
- Risk (`risk`) [within Reliability, Economics]: Uncertainty, fragility, and systems that fail in ways nobody planned for, from markets to theme parks to production.
- Existential risk (`existential-risk`) [within Risk, Policy]: Technologies that could end or permanently cripple civilisation, from nuclear weapons to misaligned AI, and how people have tried to contain them.
- AI alignment (`ai-alignment`) [within Machine learning, Existential risk]: Making AI systems pursue what their builders and users actually intend, and what happens when they do not.
- Legibility (`legibility`) [within Complex systems, Metrics, Observability]: Making a complex system readable from above: what the measure captures, what it erases, and what breaks when the map replaces the territory.
- Research labs (`research-labs`) [within History of science, History of technology]: The institutions where discovery happens and how they are funded and run: CERN, Bell Labs, ARPA, Los Alamos, DeepMind, and the labs behind modern medicine.
- Medicine (`medicine`) [within Life sciences]: How treatments are discovered, tested, and brought to patients, from antisepsis and sulfa drugs to modern drug design.
- Compilers (`compilers`) [within Programming languages]: Turning programs into other programs: parsers, interpreters, type checkers, and code generation.
- Networking (`networking`) [within Distributed systems, The open web]: How machines talk: packets, protocols, sockets, and the networks from ARPANET to the web that carry them.
- Geopolitics (`geopolitics`) [within History, Geography]: How geography, empires, and arms shape the balance of power between states and regions, as history.
- Social reform (`social-reform`) [within Economics, Policy]: Plans to redesign society or the economy, from nineteenth-century utopias to high-modernist states and basic income, and what happened when they met people.
- World history (`world-history`) [within History, Geography]: History told at the scale of continents and millennia: why societies diverged, and how the world came to look the way it does.
- Emergence (`emergence`) [within Complex systems]: Order nobody designed: reefs, the early web, neuron cultures, and simulated worlds where simple rules add up to behaviour no single part has.
- High modernism (`high-modernism`) [within Legibility, Social reform]: The confidence that society can be planned from above by experts: Le Corbusier's rational city, scientific forestry, and the schemes that failed when they met real life.
- Hubris (`hubris`) [within Risk, Ethics]: When builders overestimate their control: an island of cloned dinosaurs, cities planned on paper, the bomb, and systems more capable than their makers understand.
- The commons (`commons`) [within The open web, Economics]: Resources held in common and the rules that keep them so: common land, open protocols, open data, and the web before the platforms.
- Intellectual property (`intellectual-property`) [within Policy, Economics]: Patents, copyright, and licences: who owns an invention or a text, from the web given to the public domain to books scraped for training data.
- Provenance (`provenance`) [within Training data, Applied security]: Where something came from and who vouches for it: signed media, rights-clear training data, and artifacts that carry their own history.
- External memory (`external-memory`) [within Knowledge management, Context engineering]: Notes, links, and stores that remember for us: second brains, the web as a shared memory, and what agents write down for their next session.
- Augmentation (`augmentation`) [within AI-assisted engineering, Intelligence]: Computers that extend what people can do instead of replacing them: Licklider's symbiosis, Kasparov's centaur chess, and working alongside coding agents.
- Technology races (`technology-races`) [within Geopolitics, Existential risk]: Powers racing to build a technology first, from the bomb and its deterrence to frontier AI and the data it needs.
- Scientific revolutions (`scientific-revolutions`) [within Philosophy of science, History of science]: Moments when a field's picture of the world changes: the invention of modern science, molecular biology, antisepsis, and the first antibiotics.
- Cities (`cities`) [within Geography]: How cities are planned and how they actually grow: Jerusalem over three thousand years, Brasilia drawn on paper, and the rational city the web was designed against.
- Languages and translation (`languages`) [within Literature]: Human languages and moving meaning between them: translated novels, learning to read Chinese, Japanese, and Hebrew, and Europe's multilingual text.
- Europe (`europe`) [within Sovereignty, Geography]: Europe's place in technology and history: where the web was invented, what it builds and gives away, and the data and capabilities it still holds.
- Switzerland (`switzerland`) [within Europe]: The country this site is written from: CERN in Geneva, Basel, Swiss innovation as measured and as lived, and Swiss civic projects.
- Democratisation (`democratisation`) [within Augmentation, The commons]: A capability that needed money, a team, or years of training becoming available to anyone: printing, the web, and now building software by describing it.
- Future of work (`future-of-work`) [within Economics, Social reform]: What AI does to jobs and livelihoods: the interval before any post-scarcity economy, basic income against basic access, and who gets through the middle.
- Entrepreneurship (`entrepreneurship`) [within Economics]: Finding something worth building and building it: ventures, side projects, and what changes when anyone can spot an opportunity and operate a business with AI.
- Agent identity (`agent-identity`) [within Agents, Applied security]: Agents as principals of their own: identities, entitlements, credentials, budgets and audit trails provisioned like an employee's, with a human sponsor, instead of borrowed rights.
- Fractals (`fractals`) [within Complex systems, Mathematics]: Self-similar patterns that repeat at every scale, from rivers and coastlines to software, organisations and ideas; the lens behind much of this site.
- Abstraction (`abstraction`) [within Programming languages, History of technology]: Layers that let people stop thinking about the layer below, from assembly and programming languages to orchestrators and agents, and how each new layer becomes the ground for the next.
- Post-scarcity (`post-scarcity`) [within Economics, Future of work]: What changes when making things costs next to nothing: copied software, AI labour, mission-built machines, and the economies and societies that might follow.
- Determinism (`determinism`) [within Reliability, Philosophy]: Machines and institutions that do the same thing every time, what that sameness is worth, and where it breaks against an open world.
- Trust (`trust`) [within Risk, Economics]: Personal trust and system trust: why people rely on banks, procedures and software they cannot inspect, and how that reliance is earned.
- Factories (`factories`) [within Platform automation, Complex systems]: Machines that make machines: the factory pattern in code, real plants, universal constructors, and purpose-built things made on demand.

### Technologies

- WebAssembly (`webassembly`) [within The open web]: Portable, sandboxed bytecode for running native-speed code in the browser and beyond.
- Rust (`rust`) [within Programming languages]: The systems language most of the projects here are written in.
- Haskell (`haskell`) [within Programming languages]: The language that shaped how I think about types, effects, and correctness.
- OpenTelemetry (`opentelemetry`) [within Observability]: The vendor-neutral standard for traces, metrics, and logs, including the GenAI semantic conventions for model calls.
- TypeScript (`typescript`) [within Programming languages]: TypeScript on Bun, the language of the Agent Platform Handbook code.
- Elixir (`elixir`) [within Programming languages]: Elixir, Phoenix, and the BEAM for the long-running, fault-tolerant parts.
- Pingora (`pingora`) [within Edge systems, Rust]: Cloudflare's Rust framework for building proxies, the base of Zentinel.
- Kubernetes (`kubernetes`) [within Platform automation]: Container orchestration, and the question of when you actually need it.
- GPUs (`gpus`) [within Inference]: GPUs as the computer: memory shape, partitioning, and the hardware under inference.
- Linux (`linux`) [within Operating systems]: Linux distributions and system administration, Void Linux in particular.
- OpenBSD (`openbsd`) [within Operating systems]: OpenBSD and the BSD approach to correctness and simplicity.
- Zola (`zola`) [within The open web]: The static site generator this site and several project sites are built with.
- Durable execution (`durable-execution`) [within Distributed systems, Platform automation]: Workflow engines that keep long-running processes alive through crashes and deployments, with a journal of every step: Temporal, Restate and their kin.

### This site

- This site (`meta`): Posts about raskell.io itself: why it exists, how it is built, and where it is going.

## Projects

- [Zentinel](https://zentinelproxy.io): Security-first reverse proxy built to guard the free web.
- [hx](https://arcanist.sh/hx/): The Haskell toolchain in one fast binary.
- [bhc](https://arcanist.sh/bhc/): The Basel Haskell Compiler, a clean-slate compiler for the Haskell you already write.
- [Shiioo](https://shiioo.raskell.io): A virtual company of AI agents on your Mac, run from your phone.
- [Refrakt](https://refrakt.raskell.io): A convention-first web framework for Gleam.
- [Vela](https://vela.raskell.io): No-downtime app deployment on bare metal.
- [broodwar.live](https://broodwar.live): The community platform for StarCraft: Brood War competitive play, a basketball-reference.com for Brood War.
- [Die Zukunft](https://die-zukunft.ch): A Swiss movement that applies engineering principles to public life: not left, not right.
- [Human Macroscope](https://github.com/human-macroscope): A long-term interdisciplinary research project on humans and human collectives across scales, from individuals and families to institutions, cultures, and civilizations: how individual traits, roles, relations, and cultural transmission combine into emergent collective properties.
- [Chronicle of Earth](https://github.com/chronicle-of-earth): An interactive atlas of history and geopolitics, starting with 1900–2026.
- [WASM-AD](https://wasmad.raskell.io): A fantasy console standard with 32-bit handheld hardware: tile layers, sprites, palettes, and save RAM, memory-mapped inside the cartridge.
- [coconutOS](https://github.com/coconut-os/coconutOS): A hard shell for AI inference.
- [Terrarium](https://terrarium.raskell.io): A societal simulation engine where LLM-powered agents form emergent civilizations.
- [Hotaru](https://hotaru.raskell.io): Simulated neuron cultures on a 60-electrode array play Pong in your browser, as in the DishBrain experiment.
- [Kishi](https://kishi.raskell.io): Chess, shogi and Go against engines written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly.
- [Sango](https://sango.raskell.io): Edge diagnostics for the modern web.
- [Conflux](https://github.com/raskell-io/conflux): Schema-aware config state coordination.
- [Ushio](https://github.com/raskell-io/ushio): Deterministic edge traffic replay for understanding WAF and proxy behavior.
- [Driftscape](https://github.com/raskell-io/driftscape): Ambient soundscape platform.
- [robogym](https://github.com/raskell-io/robogym): Rust/Bevy PWA for training robotic agents.
- [Awesomeify](https://github.com/raskell-io/awesomeify): Index GitHub repos and generate static awesome-list sites.
- [Learn You the Web](https://learn-you-the-web.raskell.io): A friendly guide to how the web actually works.

## Apps

- [Manabi](https://manabi.raskell.io): A reading-first language-learning app for Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Hebrew.
- [Kurumi](https://kurumi.raskell.io): A local-first, AI-native second brain.
- [Paw & Claw](https://pawandclaw.raskell.io): A turn-based strategy game in the spirit of Advance Wars, fought by woodland armies.
- [Kishi](https://kishi.raskell.io): Chess, shogi and Go against engines written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly.
- [Rainbow River](https://rainbowriver.raskell.io): A fishing game in the style of the 32-bit handhelds, inspired by The Legend of the River King.
- [Terrarium](https://terrarium.raskell.io): A societal simulation engine where LLM-powered agents form emergent civilizations.
- [Hotaru](https://hotaru.raskell.io): Simulated neuron cultures on a 60-electrode array play Pong in your browser, as in the DishBrain experiment.

## Translations

The site is written in English. Some pages are also translated; a translation lives at the same path under a language prefix (/zh/about/ translates /about/), carries hreflang alternates, and is linked from its English page. Articles, reviews, notes, and talks are English only. Each language has a short index of its own.

## For agents

- Each article and note as Markdown: its URL with `.md` instead of the trailing slash, e.g. https://raskell.io/articles/the-model-is-a-dependency.md
- Each talk as Markdown too, e.g. https://raskell.io/talks/iat-13-basel.md
- [map.json](https://raskell.io/map.json): the site graph (articles, notes, talks, topics with definitions, series, categories, works from the reading log, projects, and their links)
- [garden.json](https://raskell.io/garden.json): the search index as data: every article, review, note, talk, work, project, topic, and cited link, with kinds, topics, and dates
- [links.json](https://raskell.io/links.json): every external link the writing cites, with the pages that cite it and whether it is a reference
- [reading.json](https://raskell.io/reading.json): the reading log, with status, dates, ratings, and reviews
- Search as a URL: https://raskell.io/search/?q={query}&type={article|review|note|talk|work|project|topic|link}
- [api-catalog](https://raskell.io/.well-known/api-catalog): RFC 9727 discovery of the machine-readable files
- Feeds: [RSS](https://raskell.io/rss.xml), [Atom](https://raskell.io/atom.xml), [articles](https://raskell.io/articles/rss.xml), [notes](https://raskell.io/notes/rss.xml), [reviews](https://raskell.io/categories/reviews/rss.xml), [talks](https://raskell.io/talks/rss.xml)
- In the browser: WebMCP tools (search_site, list_reading, find_links, get_current_page, get_page_markdown, get_site_index, list_topics, get_connections, cite_current_page, open_page) register when an agent exposes `document.modelContext`.
- No authentication, no rate limits ([auth.md](https://raskell.io/.well-known/auth.md)). Crawling for search, answers, and training is welcome (robots.txt Content-Signal).

## Optional

- [Tags](https://raskell.io/tags/): the topic index
